newsitem.title: USA: US SUGAR GROWERS CALL FOR MORE IMPORT RESTRICTIONS.
newsitem.headline: US SUGAR GROWERS CALL FOR MORE IMPORT RESTRICTIONS.

text.p: U.S. sugar growers have urged the Clinton administration to allow fewer imports during the 1997/98 marketing year that begins October 1.

In comments filed this week with the U.S. Agriculture Department, the growers complained that the current mechanism for determining the amount of sugar allowed into the United States under an annual import quota is too generous.
In particular, the 200,000 tonnes of the quota that was allocated in May should have been cancelled, they said.

Last year, USDA initially set the 1996/97 quota at 2.3 million tonnes--using a 15.5 percent "stocks-to-use ratio" as a goal. The stocks-to-use ratio compares sugar stocks on hand at the end of the year to annual consumption. The lower the ratio, the tighter the supply.

USDA initially allocated only 1.7 million tonnes of 1996/97 quota and said it would allocated the remaining 600,000 in tranches of 200,000 in January, March and May--assuming the projected stocks-to-use ratio in each of those months stayed below 15.5 percent.

In January, USDA projected the 1996/97 stocks-to-use ratio at 15.6 percent--just barely above the trigger level, but still high enough to cancel that month's tranche and effectively reduce the annual quota to 2.1 million tonnes.
Both the March and May tranches went ahead as planned.
"Without a doubt, the May tranche should have been cancelled," the sugarbeet growers said in their comments, noting that 1996/97 U.S. sugar demand turned out much lower than expected.
"Our estimates show that the (1997/98 sugar import quota) should be set at a minimum of 1.8 million tonnes and a maximum of 1.9 million," the sugarbeet growers said.

The intitial quota should also be reduced by about 143,000 tonnes to make up for the "excess sugar" imported this year. "This will bring supply and demand back into balance," the sugarbeet growers said.
The sugarbeet growers also urged USDA to allocate 200,000 tranches of the quota only if the projected stocks-to-use ratio falls below 13.5 percent, rather than 15.5 percent currently.

Alternatively, USDA could use a 14.5 percent trigger level and limit the tranches to 100,000 tonnes, the sugarbeet growers recommended. That would "assure that the stocks-to-use ratio does not go over the 15.5 percent ceiling," the group said.
The American Sugar Cane League, which represents Louisiana cane growers, called for an even more restrictive policy.
They urged that USDA abolish the trigger mechanism for at least one year to come up with a better system.
"The use of triggers have proven to be ineffective and open to manipulation, and in this particular case, unreliable," the cane growers said.
"Prices were weak before the May tranche was allocated and weakened further as foreign access to the market increased at a time when demand was sluggish," the group said.
If USDA insists on using a stocks-to-use ratio trigger, it "should be no higher than 13.5 percent," the cane growers said.
In any event, USDA should set the 1997/98 quota at about 1.64 million tonnes, they said.
Not surprisingly, U.S. sugar users have a different view of where the quota should be set.
They have called for a 1997/98 quota in the range of 2.2 million-2.3 million tonnes and a stocks-to-use trigger of at least 16.5 percent for determining tranche cancellations.
USDA officials have said they could announce both the size and details of the 1997/98 quota by the end of the month. However, the department's formal deadline is September 17.
((By Doug Palmer, 202 898 8341))
